summary.summary: Bristol's 2024/25 treasury outturn shows long-term debt rising to £600m (average rate 4.56%) against treasury investments of just £55m, lifting net debt by £118m to £545m — the first year of a five-year strategy that envisages up to £996m of new borrowing to fund the capital programme. The council remains substantially under-borrowed against its £969m capital financing requirement (CFR, the underlying need to borrow), funding the gap from cash rather than loans, and it complied with every treasury limit; general-fund financing costs were a moderate 7.18% of net revenue. Two watch items stand out: the £165m of new PWLB (Public Works Loan Board) debt was taken very short (about 1.2-year average life), so £70m — 12% of the book — matures within twelve months and must be rolled, and lenders called two LOBO loans in-year, the council repaying £35m at par rather than accept resets near 5.9%, leaving £35m of LOBOs (lender-option loans) at medium call risk.

signals.headline: Net debt up £118m to £545m and total borrowing to £600m in 2024/25 as £165m new PWLB drawn
signals.why: Debt is climbing at the start of a strategy that envisages up to £996m of new borrowing over 2024-2029.

signals.headline: £165m new PWLB (Feb-Mar 2025) taken at ~1.2yr average life; £70m (12%) of debt matures within 12 months at 31 Mar 2025
signals.why: A concentrated near-term maturity wall that must be refinanced at whatever rates prevail on maturity.

signals.headline: Lenders called LOBO options in-year: £10m Dexia (05/12/2024) and £25m Commerzbank (24/02/2025) repaid at par vs ~5.9% resets; £35m LOBOs remain at medium call risk
signals.why: A called LOBO is repaid at par, as both of these were. The remaining £35m is therefore a refinancing and liquidity exposure — cash to repay and funding to replace — not a rate-reset one.

news_drafts.headline: Bristol schools grant forecast £63.2m over in 2026/27; £99m High Needs Stability Grant announced
news_drafts.lead:
Bristol's Children and Young People Policy Committee, meeting on 26 November, has a forecast that the dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools, will overspend by £63.2m in 2026/27. The figure is at Period 6, and it increases the cumulative deficit to £172.5m.

The papers say the in-year overspend is driven mainly by pressures in high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. These include growth in education, health and care plans, placements in high-cost independent non-maintained schools, and delays in new specialist provision. The committee's finance report gives the forecast as a £63.3m adverse variance on a revised budget of £583.7m, a 10.9% overspend. It says the position "will be improved when the High Needs Stability Grant is received", with no amount or timing. A separate appendix says the Department for Education has closed its Safety Valve programme nationally. It says the new grant will provide £99m to Bristol after approval of its Local SEND Reform Plan. The appendix gives a projected cumulative deficit of £52.3m after offsets, and the council holds £21.2m in a separate reserve relating to the former programme.

The council's SEND education capital programme has six major projects, a capital works programme of about £53m and a target of 392 new specialist school places by 2030. The council's environmental impact assessment says it contributes to the Safety Valve programme "by expanding in-city provision and reducing reliance on external placements".
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix A P6Q2- Children & Young People Committee

news_drafts.headline: Bristol allocated £99m High Needs Stability Grant after government approves its SEND reform plan
news_drafts.lead:
Bristol has been indicatively allocated a £99m High Needs Stability Grant, covering 90% of the deficit on its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) accrued up to the end of 2025–26. The Department for Education and the Department for Health and Social Care have approved the city's local plan for special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), which is the condition for eligibility. Payment is expected on 30 November 2026.

Bristol's second-quarter monitoring paper for 2026/27 states that the grant brings its estimated cumulative deficit on the grant to £52.3m. It also forecasts a £63.2m in-year overspend, of which £54.5m is in high needs, the part that funds special educational needs. The paper attributes that to increased pupil numbers, complexity of need, inflationary and funding rate increases, and additional commissioned provision. The other three blocks are each forecast to balance in-year. The government's letter says the allocation "remains subject to change as a result of final audited outturn". It also says the partnership "is still developing" and has not yet consistently shown the maturity, grip and assurance needed to deliver reform.

Schools Forum is asked to confirm a proposal to move 0.5% of the Schools Block to the High Needs Block for 2027/28. Of the 75 of 126 schools that responded, 89% said yes. The 2027/28 formula is due for final agreement on 20 January 2027.

news_drafts.headline: Bristol expects High Needs Stability Grant to cut borrowing by about £19m this year
news_drafts.lead:
Bristol City Council expects to receive a High Needs Stability Grant, and its mid-year treasury management report says this will reduce its external borrowing by about £19m over the remainder of the year. The report estimates a £40m improvement in reserves and working capital, principally associated with the grant payment. The payment relates to the council's cumulative deficit on the dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools, and follows approval of its Local SEND (special educational needs and disabilities) Reform Plan.

Minutes of the Audit Committee's 29 September meeting record the external auditor saying the proposed grant would support 90% of the high needs deficit, the part of school funding for children with special needs, subject to government approval and conditions. The auditor said it depends on a reform plan and would not remove the need to address the underlying drivers of the deficit. A response is expected in the coming weeks, as part of a national process. The interim value for money report, the auditor's view of how the council manages its money, kept the deficit as its Key Recommendation, the highest category, because of its continued growth.

The committee was also told the accounts gave the wrong date for the statutory override, the temporary government rule that keeps a schools-funding deficit off the main balance sheet. It has been extended to March 2028, not March 2026, and the final version will be corrected.

findings.matters: Risks rated high likelihood with mitigations not yet clear are the items a finance director would expect to see crystallise or be funded in the next monitoring round.
